20248-the-necessity-of-atheism:
The Necessity of Atheism, in this 1933 printing, argues that gods began in human fear. To early man, the gods were as real as mountains and waterfalls. Spirits in drugs and wines seemed facts of the same order. Their power to heal or intoxicate proved their presence, men thought.

From such roots, the book traces belief toward doubt and reason. Its title echoes Shelley's famed student tract of the same name. Arguments cover nature, scripture, and the harm of forced belief. Readers get a blunt, clear case for unbelief from the freethought tradition.
20428-bertha-and-her-baptism:
Bertha and Her Baptism is a religious story written to teach young readers about baptism and heaven. It opens with a claim its makers held dear. Of those who have gone to heaven from this world, by far the larger part, it says, have been infants and young children.

The teaching runs through the tale of Bertha herself. Born sinners by one man's disobedience, children are born again of the Spirit, the book explains. Its early move to heaven is treated as mercy, not loss. Stories like this one filled Victorian nurseries, where faith and comfort were taught together.
21853-woman-s-work-in-the-civil-war-a-re:
Women's war work fills this 1867 record by L. P. Brockett and Mary C. Vaughan, gathered as the Civil War still raged. The gathering began in the autumn of 1863, out of a small book on the war's kind results meant for readers abroad. Henry W. Bellows of the Sanitary Commission writes the introduction. Sixteen steel engravings honor the women inside, Clara Barton among them.

The subtitle promises heroism, patriotism, and patience, and the pages deliver all three. Nurses, aid workers, teachers of freed people, and women who kept homes and farms appear in turn. Barbara Frietchie's famous defiance fronts the book. It stands as an early monument to the women the war made visible, written while their work was fresh.
21991-face-to-face-with-kaiserism:
James W. Gerard, lately America's ambassador to the German imperial court, continues his account in Face to Face with Kaiserism, published in 1918. The book follows his bestseller My Four Years in Germany, carrying the story to his return home. Gerard dedicates it to Colonel Edward M. House, statesman and friend. Facsimiles fill the plates: the Kaiser's visiting card, prison camp money, and stamps from Ruhleben camp.

Gerard shows the paper money used in prison camps and issued against German property. His subject is the system he faced for four years: the Kaiser, his court, and the machine behind them. Written while the war still raged, it is diplomacy as testimony. Gerard writes for American readers deciding what Germany under the Kaiser truly was.
22147-peter-the-hermit-a-tale-of-enthusi:
Daniel A. Goodsell, a Methodist bishop, wrote Peter the Hermit: A Tale of Enthusiasm in 1906. Peter was the ragged preacher whose sermons fired the First Crusade. Goodsell opens in the Holy Land of pilgrims' longing. The devout Christian, he writes, dreams of walking where the Master walked and praying in the garden of his agony.

From that longing Goodsell's Peter gathers his ragged army. The tale follows the march of the People's Crusade toward Jerusalem and its ruin. Goodsell treats Peter neither as saint nor fraud, but as enthusiasm made flesh. His book is part history, part sermon, aimed at church readers who loved the Crusades' great names.
22283-mind-and-motion-and-monism:
George John Romanes, Darwin's younger friend and defender, wrote Mind and Motion and Monism near the end of his life. The book appeared in 1895, after his death. Romanes quotes the old materialist claim that our feelings are only motions of matter pressing on our organs. Motion, that doctrine says, produces nothing but motion, and mind must be explained away or explained by it.

Romanes refuses the easy answer. Trained as a biologist and drawn to philosophy, he argues toward monism: mind and matter as two sides of one reality. The book joins his work on animal intelligence to the deepest question he knew. It is Victorian science thinking hard about the soul.
a-guide-to-stoicism: St. George Stock's Guide to Stoicism offers a clear path through the ancient philosophy of Zeno, Epictetus, and Marcus Aurelius. His lucid handbook serves beginners better than any other. The old wisdom — endurance, duty, and inner freedom — made plain and practical. An ideal first book on the Stoics.
an-essay-on-criticism: Alexander Pope's Essay on Criticism — source of 'a little learning is a dangerous thing' and 'to err is human' — remains the wittiest poem about poetry ever written. His polished couplets laid down the law for an age. Essential for all lovers of verse.
b09-luther-large-catechism:
Martin Luther published the Large Catechism in 1529 for pastors and teachers who had to instruct whole parishes. A catechism teaches faith by question and answer, and Luther's large one treats each part at full length. It covers the Ten Commandments, the Creed, the Lord's Prayer, baptism, and the Lord's Supper.

Luther writes with force and warmth, urging teachers never to think they have learned enough. His preface scolds lazy pastors in terms still quoted today. The book became a fixed standard of Lutheran teaching, kept among its confessional texts. Churches have used it to train clergy ever since. Few teaching books of the age match its plain strength.
b09-luther-small-catechism:
The Small Catechism of 1529 was Martin Luther's handbook for the home, his Enchiridion for heads of households. Where the Large Catechism served pastors, this small one fits in a hand and a memory. It gives the Ten Commandments, the Creed, and the Lord's Prayer in short form.

Baptism, confession, and the Lord's Supper follow, each with brief, clear answers to set questions. Morning and evening prayers and a Table of Duties for each place in life close the book. Luther meant fathers to teach it at table, week by week. It became the most printed Lutheran text after the Bible, and children still learn it today.

A compact account of humanity's greatest religious idea, from Abraham to the philosophers who reasoned their way to one God.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-mormonism: Mormonism began with Joseph Smith's golden plates in 1830 and became one of America's most distinctive religions. This entry surveys its history, doctrines, and polygamous past from the Catholic perspective. The American-born faith, examined from outside: the entry traces its rise from Palmyra to Utah.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-mysticism: Mysticism is the soul's direct experience of God, and this entry surveys its history, its psychology, and its great witnesses across the Christian centuries. The heart of religion, examined with care: the entry weighs its psychology, its dangers, and its fruits.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-naturalism: Naturalism denies the supernatural and makes nature the whole of reality. This entry examines its forms, its arguments, and the Catholic critique. The philosophy that closes heaven: the entry answers its claims point by point with scholastic rigor and clarity.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-naturism: Naturism is the worship of nature itself, and this entry traces its forms from primitive animism to modern pantheism. A Catholic scholar's survey of humanity's oldest temptation. The creature adored instead of the Creator: the entry traces it from animism to pantheism.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-neo-platonism: Neo-Platonism was the last great philosophy of antiquity, Plotinus's vision of all reality flowing from the One. This entry traces its system, its influence on the Fathers, and its long afterlife. Paganism's most spiritual philosophy: Augustine read it on his road to conversion.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-neo-scholasti: Neo-Scholasticism was the 19th-century revival of Aquinas, blessed by Leo XIII's Aeterni Patris in 1879. This entry traces its leaders, its method, and its triumph in Catholic schools. The old philosophy, made new: its journals and universities spread across the world.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-nestorius-and: Nestorius denied that Mary is the Mother of God, and the Council of Ephesus condemned him in 431. This entry explains his doctrine, his trial, and the far-flung Nestorian church that carried Christianity to China. The heresy that reached the Pacific.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-nihilism: Nihilism was the Russian creed that denied everything, from God to morality to the state. This entry examines its origins, its doctrines, and the Catholic critique. The philosophy of the void: its bombs shook the tsar's empire in the 1800s.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-nominalism-re: Do universals exist? Nominalists said no, realists said yes, and conceptualists split the difference, in the great medieval debate. This entry explains the positions, the combatants, and the stakes. The battle over the reality of ideas: Aquinas steered between the extremes.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-novatian-and-: Novatian was the rigorist antipope whose schism refused forgiveness to the lapsed, and his sect lasted for centuries. This entry explains his doctrine, his following, and the Church's reply. Mercy denied, and its long shadow: his rigor haunted the Church for centuries.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-occasionalism: Occasionalism teaches that God alone truly causes anything, with creatures as mere occasions. This entry explains Malebranche's system, its arguments, and the critiques. The philosophy that made God the only actor: its critics called it the death of nature itself.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-occult-art-oc: Occultism is the claim to hidden powers and secret knowledge, from magic to theosophy. This entry surveys its history, its forms, and the Church's condemnation. The forbidden arts, exposed: the entry distinguishes magic, spiritism, and theosophy with great scholarly care.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ontologism: Ontologism taught that we see God directly in every act of knowing, and Rome condemned it. This entry explains the system, its authors, and its censure. The philosophy that looked too high: Rome condemned its claim to see God directly.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-optimism: Optimism is the doctrine that this is the best of all possible worlds, taught by Leibniz. This entry explains the system, its arguments, and the Catholic critique. The philosophy of the best: the entry answers Voltaire's mocking Candide with care.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-origen-and-or: Origen was the dazzling Alexandrian whose genius shaped Christian theology and whose errors were condemned. This entry covers his life, his works, and the long controversy. The Church's most brilliant might-have-been: his Hexapla mapped the Scriptures in six parallel columns.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-paganism: Paganism is the world of the old gods, and this long entry surveys its religions, its philosophy, and its encounter with the Gospel. The darkness before the dawn: the entry maps the old gods' vast and varied ancient dominion fully.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-palm-in-chris: The palm is the Christian symbol of victory, laid before martyrs and the triumphant Christ. This entry traces its use in art, liturgy, and the catacombs. The tree of the conquerors: its branches crowned the martyrs and holy virgins alike.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-panpsychism: Panpsychism is the doctrine that all things have some degree of mind or soul. This entry explains the theory, its forms, and the Catholic critique. The philosophy that thinks everything thinks: the entry traces it from the ancient Greek philosophers.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pantheism: Pantheism identifies God with the universe, and this entry examines its forms from the Stoics to Spinoza, with the Catholic refutation. The error that drowns God in the world: the entry refutes its bold claims quite systematically and fully here.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-parallelism: Parallelism is the rhyming of thoughts that makes Hebrew poetry sing, line answering line. This entry explains its forms, its beauty, and its use. The psalms' native music: their parallel lines still sing so sweetly in every single human tongue.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pelagius-and-: Pelagius denied original sin and made man his own savior, and Augustine crushed his heresy. This long entry explains the doctrine, the controversy, and the condemnation. The heresy of self-salvation: its crushing defeat forever defined the Catholic doctrine of grace.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pessimism: Pessimism is the philosophy that life is not worth living. This entry examines its systems, from Schopenhauer to Hartmann, and the Catholic answer. The doctrine of despair, refuted: the entry answers it firmly with bright and certain Catholic hope indeed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pestalozzi-an: Pestalozzi was the Swiss educator who taught that love is the soul of teaching. This entry covers his schools, his method, and his Catholic critics. The father of the modern school: his famous Yverdon institute drew the admiring world's gaze.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-phenomenalism: Phenomenalism is the philosophy that we know only appearances, never things themselves. This entry examines its systems, from Hume to Mill, and the Catholic critique. The doctrine of the veil of sense: its denial of substance ends in bleak scepticism.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-philanthropin: Philanthropinism was Basedow's 1700s movement to educate children by nature and reason. This entry explains its schools, its methods, and the Catholic judgment on it. The enlightenment's schoolroom: its famous Dessau institute was the celebrated model school of the age.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pietism: Pietism was the Lutheran movement that sought a religion of the heart against dead orthodoxy. This entry explains its founders, its forms, and the Catholic judgment. The heart's revolt in Protestantism: its fervent conventicles spread across all Protestant Germany and beyond.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-plato-and-pla: Plato's philosophy shaped Christian thought more than any other pagan system. This long entry examines his dialogues, his ideas, and his influence on the Fathers. The philosopher of the eternal forms: his haunting cave allegory still troubles the schools today.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-polytheism: Polytheism is the worship of many gods, humanity's oldest error. This entry examines its forms, its causes, and the Catholic refutation. The many gods that are no gods: their dumb idols fell silent before the fearless preaching of the Gospel.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-positivism: Positivism is Comte's system that banished metaphysics for science. This entry examines its doctrines, its religion of humanity, and the Catholic refutation. The philosophy that worshipped man: its strange high priest was Auguste Comte himself in Paris's positivist temple of humanity.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-poverty-and-p: Poverty and pauperism are the social wounds the Church has always tended. This entry examines their causes, their remedies, and the Catholic teaching. The problem of the poor: its true answer is organized Christian charity in daily action for souls.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pragmatism: Pragmatism is the philosophy that judges truth by its works. This entry examines its founders, its doctrines, and the Catholic critique. The test of the cash value: its clever pragmatists doubted that the absolute truth itself had ever really existed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-predestinaria: Predestinarianism is the heresy that denied man's free will. This entry traces its teachers, its condemnations, and its errors. The denial of the will's freedom: its dark error chained the helpless human soul in iron fate forevermore in hopeless darkness.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-presbyteriani: Presbyterianism is the Calvinist system of church rule by elders. This entry examines its doctrines, its history, and the Catholic judgment. The kirk of the Scots: its stern General Assembly rules in Edinburgh's High Kirk today still in solemn session.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-priscillianis: Priscillianism was the Spanish heresy of the fourth century. This entry traces its doctrines, its councils, and its condemnation. The ascetic heresy of the West: its condemned bishops died at Trier in 385's cold autumn winds of Gaul's far frontier.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-probabilism: Probabilism is the moral system that follows a probable opinion. This entry examines its doctrine, its defenders, and its opponents. The liberty of the doubtful conscience: its great masters were the learned Jesuits of olden days gone by in Spain.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-protestantism: Protestantism is the great schism of the sixteenth century. This long entry examines its origins, its divisions, and the Catholic judgment. The revolt of the reformers: its endless divisions number the warring sects today still multiplying in endless strife and schism.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-psycho-physic: Psycho-physical parallelism is the theory that mind and body run side by side. This entry examines its forms and the Catholic critique. The two clocks of the soul: their twin hands never truly touch in the theory's rigid scheme of mind.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pusey-and-pus: Puseyism was the Oxford Movement's Catholic revival. This entry traces Pusey's life, the Tracts, and the Catholic judgment. The high church road to Rome: its famous Tracts stirred sleepy Oxford's dons to anger and learned debate in print and pulpit.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pyrrhonism: Pyrrhonism is the ancient philosophy of universal doubt. This entry examines its founder, its tropes, and the Catholic refutation. The suspension of all judgment: its smiling sage doubted everything in life and in thought alike in ancient Elis of Greece.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pythagoras-an: Pythagoras was the sage of numbers and the transmigrating soul. This entry examines his life, his school, and his influence. The philosopher of the harmony: his great theorem rules the schools of geometry today still unchallenged in proof and use.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-quietism: Quietism is the heresy of passive prayer that abandoned effort. This entry traces Molinos, its condemnation, and its errors. The rest that renounced the will: its condemned errors died in 1687's papal decree Coelestis Pastor forevermore in Rome itself in print.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-rabbi-and-rab: Rabbi and Rabbinism are the teachers and tradition of Judaism. This entry examines their origin, their schools, and their literature. The masters of the Law: their vast Talmud fills the crowded shelves of study and prayer and law and lore.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-rationalism: Rationalism is the philosophy that enthroned reason above faith. This entry examines its forms, its masters, and the Catholic refutation. The revolt of the unaided mind: its proud systems denied the Christian mysteries of faith and grace and hope and heaven.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-relativism: Relativism is the doctrine that truth changes with the mind. This entry examines its forms and the Catholic refutation. The philosophy of the shifting standard: its crooked measure bends with fickle men and changing times and moods and fashions and whims.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-religious-ind: Religious indifferentism is the error that all faiths are equal. This entry examines its forms and the Catholic condemnation. The denial of the one true Church: its proud error levels the faiths of men in folly and pride and blindness.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ritschlianism: Ritschlianism is the theology of Albrecht Ritschl's school. This entry examines its doctrines and the Catholic refutation. The kingdom without the King: its cold ethics displaced the dogma of Christ the Lord and God and Man and Savior and King.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-roman-catechi: The Roman Catechism is the Trent's manual for parish priests. This entry examines its origin, its doctrine, and its influence. The book of the Council's mind: its weighty pages teach the priests of the world in Latin and the vernacular.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-rosmini-and-r: Antonio Rosmini was the philosopher-priest of Rovereto. This entry examines his system, his condemnation, and his vindication. The thinker of the ideal being: his profound books shaped the schools of Italy's north in the 1830s' decades of thought and prayer.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sabbatarians-: The Sabbatarians are the keepers of the Saturday Sabbath. This entry examines their sects, their doctrines, and the Catholic judgment. The observers of the seventh day: their scattered sects keep the Saturday Sabbath in the 1600s' England of the Civil War.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-saint-simon-a: Saint-Simon was the prophet of the industrial order. This entry examines his doctrine, his disciples, and the Church's judgment. The utopian of the new Christianity: his ardent school dreamed the future in Paris in the 1820s' salons of the left.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-scepticism: Scepticism is the doubt of the knowable. This long entry examines its kinds, its history, and the Church's answer. The philosophy of the suspended judgment: its cold doubt questions all in the schools of the age in the 1700s' salons.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-schism: Schism is the rent in the Church's unity. This long entry examines its nature, its kinds, and its history. The separation of the disobedient: its sad rent divides the flock in the Church of Christ in schism's wound in the body.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-scholasticism: Scholasticism is the philosophy of the schools. This very long entry examines its method, its masters, and its history. The reasoned faith of the Middle Ages: its great masters crowned Paris in the 1200s' schools of the university in the city.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-secularism: Secularism is the creed of the world without God. This entry examines its doctrines, its prophets, and the Church's answer. The philosophy of the closed horizon: its cold creed denies the altar in the 1800s' schools of the West in the cities.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-semiarians-an: The Semiarians were the half-way Arians. This entry examines their creeds, their councils, and their end. The heresy of the middle party: its wavering creeds died in the 300s in the East's councils in the provinces of the empire in Asia.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-semipelagiani: Semipelagianism is the error of the half-grace. This entry examines its doctrines, its monks, and its condemnation. The heresy of the Marseilles theologians: its subtle error died in the 500s in Gaul's monasteries in the south of the province in Lérins.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-shamanism: Shamanism is the religion of the spirit-men. This entry examines its rites, its peoples, and its errors. The sorcery of the northern tribes: its wild drums call the spirits in the steppes of Asia in the north of the continent.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sikhism: Sikhism is the religion of the Punjab's Gurus. This entry examines its ten masters, its book, and its creed. The faith of the Khalsa brotherhood: its ten Gurus taught the Punjab in the 1500s' villages in the north of India.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-socialism: Socialism is the creed of the common ownership. This long entry examines its schools, its errors, and the Church's judgment. The doctrine of the collectivist state: its many schools filled the 1800s in Europe's cities in the factories of the north.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-socinianism: Socinianism is the heresy of the Polish Brethren. This entry examines its doctrines, its Racovian, and its end. The anti-Trinitarians of the Reformation: their famed catechism filled Raków in the 1600s' Poland in the Commonwealth of the nobles in the sejm.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-spiritism: Spiritism is the traffic with the dead. This entry examines its séances, its errors, and the Church's judgment. The fraud of the darkened room: its turning tables filled the 1850s in the salons of the credulous in the cities of the West.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-spiritualism: Spiritualism is the philosophy of the spirit's primacy. This entry examines its schools, its doctrines, and its errors. The idealism of the modern mind: its many schools filled the 1800s in the universities of the West in the faculties of the mind.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-symbolism: Symbolism is the language of sacred signs. This long entry examines its liturgy, its art, and its meaning. The speech of the veiled mysteries: its holy signs filled the liturgy in the 400s of the Church in the basilicas of the city.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-syncretism: Syncretism is the mixture of religions. This entry traces its philosophy and its danger. The blending of the incompatible faiths: its grave errors filled the apologetics in the 200s of the Fathers in the books of the very old apologists.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-syndicalism: Syndicalism is the movement of the trade unions. This entry traces its Sorel, its strikes, and its doctrine. The revolt of the working class: its great strikes filled the factories in the 1900s' France in the towns of the north.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-taoism: Taoism is the religion of the Way. This long entry examines its Laozi, its immortals, and its history. The philosophy of the Chinese sages: its mystic Way crowned the mountains in the 400s BC of the sages in the valleys.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-the-lamb-in-e: The Lamb is the symbol of Christ. This entry traces its catacombs, its Agnus, and its meaning. The emblem of the sacrificed Lord: its carved form crowned the catacombs in the 100s of the martyrs in the very old tombs.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-thomism: Thomism is the school of Aquinas. This very long entry examines its 1200s, its Summa, and its history. The philosophy of the Angelic Doctor: its great Summa crowned Paris in the 1270s of the Dominicans in the very old schools.
doe-osti-2997177-operational-forecasting: Predicting human-caused earthquakes got its DOE forecaster, and this CRADA final tunes the warning system. The pages log the prediction trials. The geophysicists get their closeout. The quakes were induced. The trials were prediction. The closeout was geophysicist. The system was warning.
doe-osti-3018774-feasibility-and-qualita: Fuel cell buses got airport-backup-assessed, and this DOE text studies emergency power. The pages detail the risk findings. The transport folks get their data. The use was backup power. The data were transport. The power was emergency. The assessment was risk.
doe-osti-3409108-the-hawaii-meteorology-: Hawaii MET got toolkit-built, and this DOE toolkit covers meteorology energy transmission. The pages detail the Hawaii findings. The energy folks get their data. The toolkit was transmission. The data were energy. The MET were Hawaii. The transmission were toolkit.
english-literary-criticism: Scholar Charles Edwyn Vaughan assembled key examples of English literary criticism, letting the great critics speak for themselves. Readers meet centuries of argument about what makes poetry and prose good, from the Renaissance to the modern age. The collection serves students and general readers alike as a guided tour through the changing standards by which English books have been judged.
govdocs-archive_org-VealeFJPAdvanceToBar:
F. J. P. Veale, an English solicitor and writer, published Advance to Barbarism to trace how warfare became total between Sarajevo and Hiroshima. His span runs from the First World War's opening shots to the atomic bombing of Japan in 1945.

Veale argues that modern war shed its old limits step by step, until bombing cities and killing civilians became normal practice, and he lays much of the blame on the Allied side. The book became a staple of revisionist history and is still hotly debated. It is held as an archive item, without endorsement, for readers weighing its charges.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-Patriotism_Patr: Titled simply 'Patriotism,' this declassified US government document sits in the Internet Archive's govdocs set. What it says about patriotism - or who wrote it, and when - the catalog does not say. No public text has been located. A title in search of its contents.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-Vandalism_Vanda: nsia-Vandalism Vandalism: the made public government document, captured as titled. Subject: government records. A bare file, kept as issued. An obscure item, complete, filed. From the archive shelves, for readers of the files and readers.
mediaeval-socialism:
Bede Jarrett wrote Mediaeval Socialism, printed in London and New York. Jarrett was a Dominican friar, marked by the initials O.P. Seven chapters and a book list make up the short work.

An intro sets the scene, then social conditions in the middle ages. Chapters treat the communists, the schoolmen, and the lawyers of that age. Social reformers get a chapter of their own near the end. The last chapter weighs the old theory of giving alms to the poor. A full index closes the book for students who cite it. Jarrett writes as both a friar and a trained scholar.
mill-utilitarianism:
John Stuart Mill published Utilitarianism in 1863, his clear short statement of the moral theory he inherited from Jeremy Bentham and his father. The book first ran as essays in Fraser's Magazine in 1861. Mill meant it as the theory's best case, not a textbook.

The creed is simple: acts are right as they add to happiness, wrong as they add to pain. Mill answers the stock attacks: that the rule is a pig's philosophy, too cold, or too hard to use. He ranks pleasures of mind above those of body, and grounds justice in utility. The book remains the theory's standard statement.
moulton-early-zoroastrianism:
James Hope Moulton's Early Zoroastrianism appeared in 1913 as Hibbert Lectures. The Manchester scholar gives the classic English study of the prophet. Zoroaster's faith, among the oldest prophetic faiths, fills his pages.

Moulton traces the Gathas, the hymns held to be Zoroaster's own words. The stark duel of good and evil stands at the faith's core. He weighs the faith's long sway on Jews, Christians, and others. Learning sits lightly in prose a plain reader can follow with ease. Many still call the book the best first guide to the whole subject. Moulton's fairness toward a faith not his own wins trust fast.
nasa-tm-19650024111-dipole-resonances-in:
Peter A Sturrock, of Ames Research Center and Stanford's Institute for Plasma Research, studied resonances in a magnetized plasma. Radar soundings from a satellite above the ionosphere had shown such resonances. A dipole antenna can excite them and can also detect them. A plasma is resonant, Sturrock explains, when the group velocity for a mode falls to zero.

His treatment is theoretical and treats the dipole as vanishingly small. The plasma is taken as uniform, or homogeneous, throughout. Ionosphere soundings from satellites were new at the time. Explaining their odd echoes required exactly this kind of careful wave theory, tied to a real instrument in orbit.
nasa-tm-19690009834-the-sdp-3-a-computer:
R. A. Cliff of Goddard Space Flight Center describes the SDP-3, a computer built for small scientific spacecraft, in this paper. Spacecraft radios can only send limited data to Earth. Cliff argues for raising the worth of each transmitted bit instead of just sending more bits.

The SDP-3 is a general-purpose stored-program computer meant as the core of a small spacecraft data system. It processes data on board and removes redundancy before transmission. Removing redundancy in space can use less power than sending the raw data. The machine uses serial, two's complement arithmetic with sixteen-bit words. A sixteen-level priority interrupt system supports time-sharing operation aboard the spacecraft.
nasa-tm-19690025525-the-feasibility-of-w:
William J. Robinson Jr., of the Space Sciences Laboratory at Marshall Space Flight Center, wrote this revised report, TM X-53806, dated May 27, 1969. He studies the feasibility of beaming power wirelessly to an orbiting astronomical station. A station fed from outside could avoid carrying all of its own power generation gear into orbit.

Two beaming methods are worked through in full: microwaves and lasers. For each, Robinson covers power generation, transmission across space, and reception with conversion back to electricity. Overall microwave efficiencies get their own summary section. A head-to-head comparison then weighs the two methods stage by stage. Artist's drawings show the station under each kind of beam before the conclusions chapter.
podcast-dannyjones-8jksrbKGGSM:
Travis Kitchens returns to Danny Jones's podcast with a claim pitched at full volume. Billionaires, he says, are secretly funding a psychedelic holy war. In his account they bankroll the spread of mind-altering drugs as a spiritual and political project. Kitchens connects foundations, research money, and the psychedelic revival into one design.

Jones works through the money trail with him, name by name. The revival itself is real and well funded, and readers can verify its donors; the holy war framing is Kitchens's interpretation of that money's purpose. The episode keeps the two separate in presentation even when the guest merges them. For listeners tracking how psychedelics moved from counterculture to boardrooms, the conversation offers a suspicious, detailed, and arguable map of who paid for the trip.
podcast-dannyjones-JMR7_5SSWsM:
Whitley Strieber wrote Communion, the bestselling account of his own abduction experiences, and changed how America pictured aliens. With Danny Jones, the most famous abduction witness alive discusses human-alien hybrids said to live among us, and what he believes the visitors intend for humanity.

Strieber has told his story for nearly forty years, refining a theology of the encounter along the way. Jones questions him as a seeker rather than a skeptic, and Strieber answers with the calm of a man long past caring who believes him. No evidence settles his claims, and the episode offers testimony instead. Its preservation value is cultural: the founding witness of the modern abduction era, speaking at length in his own late style, for the audience that inherited his imagery.
podcast-dannyjones-j_gMP1TgFsM:
Con artist Matthew Cox joins Danny Jones for a true-crime talk billed around the Gabby Petito case. The title asks if her fiance was a psychopath. Cox knows fraud and prison from the inside.

The sample opens on Cox's own new film about a con man contest in Europe. It then turns to the Theranos trial of Elizabeth Holmes. Cox gives a fraudster's read on lies, charm, and self-belief. The Petito question frames the hour, but Cox's own past gives the talk its sharp, uneasy edge throughout. Listeners get both crime analysis and showmanship.
podcast-joerogan-cdP3L73yySM:
Commentator Hotep Jesus sits with Rogan for episode 1318 of the Joe Rogan Experience. Known for blunt online broadcasts, he brings an unfiltered take on race, culture, and the internet's wars. The talk is fiery by design, and Rogan lets it run hot.

The two argue and joke their way across the subjects that built his following, from media narratives to personal responsibility. Rogan pushes back where the claims stretch and laughs where they land. The episode preserves a provocative voice at full volume, the kind of guest booking that made the young show a free-speech landmark for its fans.
podcast-joerogan-p6LJXPOv4SM:
Robert F. Kennedy Jr. sits with Joe Rogan for episode 1999, recorded while Kennedy was running for president. Kennedy, an environmental lawyer from the famous political family, had broken with the Democratic Party. The long talk gave his campaign one of its biggest platforms.

Kennedy lays out his views on vaccines, public health agencies, and corporate power over government. He also talks about the environment and the legacy of his father and uncle, both killed in the 1960s. Rogan lets him speak at length with few interruptions. The episode became a key moment in Kennedy's run and in Rogan's political reach.
podcast-joerogan-qSLs1-KwasM:
Graham Hancock returns to the Joe Rogan Experience for episode 2215 with fresh claims about a lost Ice Age civilization. Hancock, author of Fingerprints of the Gods, argues that a comet strike wiped out an advanced culture. His Netflix series made that case to millions.

Hancock updates Rogan on sites and finds he says support his theory. He attacks the archaeology establishment for refusing to debate him fairly. Rogan, his most loyal platform, lets him lay out the full argument at length. The episode shows how Hancock's once-fringe ideas now reach a mass audience first.
podcast-tuckercarlson-tFM6L6TopsM:
Political strategist Steve Bannon joins Tucker Carlson after Israel strikes Iran. Both men oppose deeper American involvement in the war. They warn the fight could split the movement that backed Donald Trump.

Bannon argues that a long war would drain support among working-class voters. Carlson agrees that foreign wars have hurt past presidents and parties. They discuss pressure from donors, media voices, and party leaders. The episode captures a sharp split inside the American right over Israel, Iran, and the limits of loyalty to Trump. Neither man hides how deep his doubts about the war run.
poems-of-american-patriotism: Editor Brander Matthews gathered verse celebrating American history and ideals, from the Revolution through his own day. The anthology mixes famous battle poems and anthems with lesser-known pieces honoring soldiers, statesmen, and the flag. Arranged for schools and family reading, it offers a window into how early-twentieth-century Americans wanted their children to feel about their country.
poems-of-optimism: Ella Wheeler Wilcox sings optimism — cheer, courage, kindness, and the power of glad thought — in verses that lifted millions. Her sunny faith in life's goodness never wavers. The poet of hope at her brightest and best. Her brave gladness has cheered readers for over a century.
the-soul-of-man-under-socialism: Oscar Wilde's 1891 essay arguing that socialism's true goal should be individualism: freeing people from drudgery so each can become an artist of his own life. Paradoxical, witty, and utopian, it is Wilde's most serious political writing. Beautifully argued and still provocative, it shows the philosopher behind the wit.
